rejected.title: First Nations exchange networks
card: For thousands of years, First Nations communities traded goods with each other along trade routes. Some routes stretched across much of the continent.
Goods included ochre (a coloured earth used for painting and ceremony), stone for tools, and food. A good could be carried far from the place it came from.
Resources were also shared through kinship ties. Kinship is a system of family relationships that sets out what people owe and give each other.
Trade and sharing let communities get goods their own area lacked. Groups who cared for a quarry often controlled who could take from it, so resources were used with care.
rejected.remember: Goods travelled along trade routes, and kinship set out who shared what with whom.

a.q: What is kinship, as part of First Nations exchange networks?
opts: A system of family ties that sets what people share
A long path that goods travel along between areas
A coloured earth used for painting and ceremony
A payment in coins made for goods from far away
a.why: Kinship is a system of family relationships that sets out what people owe and give each other, so resources were shared along those ties. A path that goods travel along is a trade route, which is a different part of the network.
a.clue: Think about how people are related to each other.

b.q: Stone from one quarry is found at a campsite hundreds of kilometres away, where no such stone occurs. What does this most likely show?
opts: The stone was carried there along a trade route
The stone formed at the campsite over time
The quarry had no rules about who took stone
The campsite's people had no need for stone
b.why: No such stone occurs near the campsite, so it must have come from somewhere else. Goods such as stone were carried long distances along trade routes. The stone could not have formed at the campsite, because none is found there.
b.clue: Where did the stone come from?

version.title: First Nations exchange networks
card: For tens of thousands of years, First Nations communities traded goods along trade routes. Some routes linked groups thousands of kilometres apart.
Goods included ochre (a coloured earth used in painting and ceremony), stone for tools, and food. Trade let a group get goods its own area did not have.
Resources were also shared through kinship. Kinship is a system of family relationships that sets out what each person gives to and gets from others.
Resources were limited, so they were used with care. Law often set who could take stone from a quarry or food from an area, and when.
version.remember: Trade and kinship moved and shared limited resources, and law guided their careful use.

a.q: How did kinship help First Nations communities share resources?
opts: It set what relatives gave to and got from each other
It marked the paths that goods travelled between groups
It set a price in coins for each good that was traded
It let each family keep all it gathered for itself
a.why: Kinship is a system of family relationships that sets out what each person gives and gets, so resources moved between relatives. The paths goods travelled along are trade routes, a different part of the network.
a.clue: Kinship is about how people are related.

b.q: A group lives where there is good ochre but little stone for making sharp tools. Using the exchange networks, how could they most likely get good stone?
opts: Trade ochre for stone with groups along a route
Use ochre for tools, since it is a kind of stone
Take stone from any quarry they find, with no rules
Go without stone, as goods were never carried far
b.why: Trade let a group get goods its own area lacked, so ochre could be traded for stone along a trade route. Taking stone from any quarry does not fit, because law often set who could take from a quarry and when.
b.clue: What does the group have that others might want?

a.best: It set what relatives gave to and got from each other

b.best: Trade ochre for stone with groups along a route

problems.detail: Trade, sharing through kinship and Law are all written in the past tense ("were shared", "Law often set"), which can suggest kinship obligations and Law over Country ended. They continue in many communities today; a short line saying so, or present tense for kinship and Law, would avoid that reading.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer and the facts are sound. The card puts kinship and Law only in the past tense, which could suggest they no longer exist; the dating of long-distance trade routes to tens of thousands of years is broad and worth a quick look.
